reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Static load testing is the most accurate method of determining pile load capacity; tests may be done in the design or construction stage, and the conventional types are axial compression, axial tension and lateral.
sections.body: 9.1 General (p. 1). Static load testing of piles is the most accurate method of determining load capacity. Depending on project size and other variables, static load tests may be performed in the design stage or construction stage. Conventional types are axial compression, axial tension and lateral load tests. The chapter gives an overview of static testing, its importance, and the basic test methods and interpretation; for more detail see the publications at the end of the chapter, including the most recent ASTM standards and the NYSDOT Static Pile Load Test Manual, GCP-18 (2007).
key_points: Static load test: the most accurate method of determining pile load capacity
Design-stage or construction-stage tests; axial compression, axial tension and lateral types
Details: current ASTM standards and NYSDOT Static Pile Load Test Manual GCP-18 (2007)
sections.applicability: Planning a driven pile static load test program and its LRFD resistance factors.

sections.title: Reasons and Prerequisites for a Static Load Test Program
sections.summary: Reasons for static load tests (design and construction verification, confirming nominal resistance, calibrating resistance factors, p-y response) and prerequisites (subsurface exploration, stratigraphy, static analyses).
sections.body: 9.1.1 Reasons and Prerequisites for a Static Load Test Program (pp. 1 to 2). Static load testing gives design verification information on nominal resistance and deformation response of test or production piles. Reasons: (1) design verification or refinement and construction verification or procedure modification from measured load-deflection or load-transfer data; (2) confirm the subsurface materials provide the nominal geotechnical resistance; (3) determine or calibrate resistance factors for new static design methods, local or regional geologic conditions, or dynamic or rapid load test analysis methods; (4) determine p-y response of laterally loaded piles. Program development and oversight should be by an experienced foundation engineer; static tests are often a comparison baseline, and quality is of utmost importance for research or updating LRFD resistance factors, since poorly performed tests can give unsafe or grossly uneconomical foundations. Before planning, obtain: (1) a detailed subsurface exploration at the test location (a load test is not a substitute for it); (2) well defined stratigraphy with engineering parameters and groundwater conditions; (3) static analyses to select pile type(s), length(s) and test location(s).
key_points: Reasons: design/construction verification, confirm nominal resistance, calibrate resistance factors, p-y response
An experienced foundation engineer should develop and oversee the program
A load test is not a substitute for a subsurface exploration program
Prerequisites: exploration at the test location, stratigraphy and groundwater, static analyses
sections.applicability: Deciding why and when a driven pile static load test program is needed and what must precede it.

sections.title: Developing a Static Load Test Program
sections.summary: Planning items for a static load test program: loading apparatus able to reach geotechnical failure (jack and load cell 120% to 150% of the maximum load), load cell and spherical bearing plate, gages with enough travel, experienced supervision, a full installation record and dynamic monitoring.
sections.body: 9.1.2 Developing a Static Load Test Program (pp. 2 to 3). Set the goal and objectives first; confirming nominal resistance needs far less effort and instrumentation than detailed load transfer for final design. Items: (1) loading apparatus (reaction system and jack) able to load the pile to geotechnical nominal resistance; one sized only for the anticipated nominal resistance usually cannot reach geotechnical failure, so the full benefit is lost; jack capacity 120% to 150% of the anticipated maximum load. (2) Specify a load cell and spherical bearing plate and LVDTs or dial gages with sufficient travel (prohibit gages that must be shimmed and reset); where possible measure movement at the toe and intermediate points; load cell capacity 120% to 150% of the maximum load. (3) Supervision by an experienced foundation engineer. (4) A full test pile installation record: hammer stroke (especially at final driving), fuel/energy setting, hammer cushion and pile cushion materials and thickness (new and replaced), accurately determined final set, installation aids such as predrilling and depths, start and end times, stopping depths and durations for splicing or maintenance. (5) Dynamic monitoring of the test pile for nominal resistance at driving with soil resistance distribution, drive system performance, driving stresses and wave equation input refinement.
key_points: Loading apparatus must be able to reach geotechnical failure, not just the anticipated nominal resistance
Jack and load cell capacity 120% to 150% of the anticipated maximum test load
Load cell, spherical bearing plate, and gages with enough travel (no shimming and resetting)
Record full installation details, not only hammer model and driving resistance
Dynamic monitoring of the load test pile recommended
sections.applicability: Planning the equipment, supervision and records of a driven pile static load test.

sections.title: When and Where to Load Test
sections.summary: Number and location of load tests follow site variability; AASHTO's static load test resistance factor assumes one test per site condition. Kyfor et al. (1992) list eleven conditions in which static load testing is effective.
sections.body: 9.1.3 When and Where to Load Test (pp. 3 to 4). Tests in either phase should achieve a set goal, usually nominal resistance or load transfer at a representative location; number and location follow site variability (Section 5.5.3, AASHTO 2014), and the AASHTO resistance factor for static load testing is based on one test per site condition. Conditions for effective use (adapted from FHWA-SA-91-042, Kyfor et al. 1992): (1) substantial cost savings, often on large projects with friction piles (shorter lengths) or end bearing piles (higher nominal resistance); (2) nominal resistance uncertain from limited experience or unusual conditions; (3) variable conditions that can be zoned, tested in representative areas; (4) significantly higher nominal resistance than typical practice; (5) significant setup or relaxation expected; (6) reliable tension or lateral deflection assessment important; (7) verifying new design or testing methods; (8) new pile types, large diameter open end pipe piles, or new installation procedures; (9) reusing existing piles for heavier loads; (10) dynamic estimates during construction differing significantly from static analysis, e.g., H-piles that 'run' in loose to medium dense sands and gravels; (11) developing local or regional LRFD calibration.
key_points: Number and location of tests follow site variability; AASHTO factor assumes one test per site condition
Effective when savings are substantial or nominal resistance is uncertain or unusually high
Also for setup or relaxation, tension or lateral needs, new methods, new pile types, reused piles
Also when dynamic and static estimates differ significantly, or for local LRFD calibration
sections.applicability: Choosing whether, how many and where to perform static pile load tests.

sections.title: Effective Use of Load Test Information
sections.summary: Load test information can be used effectively in the design stage, the construction stage and in load test databases (Sections 9.1.4.1 to 9.1.4.3).
sections.body: 9.1.4 Effective Use of Load Test Information (p. 5). The heading introduces the design stage (9.1.4.1), construction stage (9.1.4.2) and load test database (9.1.4.3) uses of load test information; it carries no text of its own.
key_points: Uses: design stage, construction stage, load test databases
sections.applicability: Overview of how static load test results are used in design, construction and databases.

sections.title: Design Stage
sections.summary: A design-phase load test program gives the best design information; its advantages include comparing pile types, confirming drivability, preliminary driving criteria, lower bid contingency and fewer disputes.
sections.body: 9.1.4.1 Design Stage (p. 5). A design-phase load testing program gives the best information for pile foundation design. The number of tests, pile types, driving method and test loads are selected cooperatively by the geotechnical and structural engineers. Advantages: (a) testing several pile types, sections and lengths to select the most economical foundation; (b) confirming drivability to minimum penetration and nominal resistance at estimated penetration depths; (c) preliminary driving criteria for production piles; (d) driving information for bidders should reduce bid 'contingency'; (e) fewer contract disputes over driving problems; (f) results reflected in the final design and specifications.
key_points: Design-stage tests give the best design information; geotechnical and structural engineers select them together
Allow comparing pile types, sections and lengths for the most economical foundation
Confirm drivability and set preliminary driving criteria; reduce bid contingency and disputes
sections.applicability: Benefits of static load testing during the design phase.

sections.title: Construction Stage
sections.summary: Construction-stage static load tests confirm design loads, set final production pile lengths and installation procedures, and refine plan lengths and minimum penetration.
sections.body: 9.1.4.2 Construction Stage (p. 5). Testing at the start of construction may be the only practical time on projects that cannot justify a design stage program. Construction stage tests confirm the design loads are appropriate, establish final design lengths for production piles, and assure the installation procedure is satisfactory; perhaps most importantly they refine the estimated pile lengths on the plans and establish minimum penetration requirements.
key_points: Construction-stage tests may be the only practical option on some projects
Confirm design loads, final production lengths and installation procedure
Refine plan pile lengths and minimum penetration requirements
sections.applicability: Benefits of static load testing at the start of construction.

sections.title: Load Test Databases
sections.summary: Load test databases support resistance factor calibration (e.g., Oregon DOT wave equation study: phi_dyn 0.55 initial driving, 0.40 restrike; AASHTO 2010 raised wave equation phi_dyn from 0.40 to 0.50); FHWA DFLTD holds about 1300 tests (1985-2003); results should be stored with full site and installation details.
sections.body: 9.1.4.3 Load Test Databases (p. 6). Load test databases (Paikowsky 2004; Abu-Hejleh 2015) are needed for design method reliability calibration and better production design; complete databases allow comparing design and construction verification methods with full scale results, possibly raising a method's resistance factor or showing preferable alternatives. Oregon DOT (2010; Smith et al. 2011) evaluated wave equation resistance factors: the AASHTO phi_dyn of 0.40 then raised costs, and the study recommended 0.55 for initial driving and 0.40 for restrikes; from this and other work AASHTO (2010) changed the wave equation phi_dyn from 0.40 to 0.50. The FHWA Deep Foundation Load Test Database (DFLTD), no longer updated but available on request, holds about 1300 load tests from 1985 to 2003; several state agencies have their own. Store results with geotechnical and installation information, using the report section of the ASTM standard for each test type as the list of details to keep.
key_points: Databases support reliability calibration of design and construction control methods
Oregon DOT: wave equation phi_dyn 0.55 initial driving, 0.40 restrike; AASHTO (2010) changed 0.40 to 0.50
FHWA DFLTD: about 1300 load tests, 1985 to 2003, available on request
Store results with full site, installation and test details per the ASTM report sections
sections.applicability: Using and maintaining pile load test databases for calibration.

sections.title: Resistance Factors for Static Load Testing
sections.summary: Table 9-1: resistance factors for nominal axial resistance from static load tests: compression phi_dyn 0.80 with dynamic testing, 0.75 without; tension phi_up 0.60. No factor for lateral tests (service limit deformation governs).
sections.body: 9.1.5 Resistance Factors for Static Load Testing (p. 7). Resistance factors for the nominal axial geotechnical resistance from a static load test are in Table 9-1; they depend on compression or tension and on whether dynamic testing is performed. No resistance factor is given for lateral load testing, which is generally controlled by service limit state deformation criteria rather than strength. Table 9-1 (modified from AASHTO 2014): nominal axial compression resistance of a single pile, phi_dyn: driving criteria established by a successful static load test of at least one pile per site condition and dynamic testing of at least two piles per site condition, but no less than 2% of production piles, 0.80; static load test of at least one pile per site condition without dynamic testing, 0.75; nominal axial tension resistance of a single pile, phi_up: static load test, 0.60.
key_points: phi_dyn 0.80: static load test plus dynamic testing of at least 2 piles per site condition (>= 2% of production piles)
phi_dyn 0.75: static load test without dynamic testing
phi_up 0.60: static tension load test
No resistance factor for lateral load tests: service limit deformation governs

sections.title: Axial Compression Load Test
sections.summary: Axial compression is the most common pile test: incremental or constant-rate loading at the head, readings of time, load and head movement, a load-movement curve, nominal resistance by an interpretation method; telltales and strain gages give load transfer.
sections.body: 9.2 Axial Compression Load Test (pp. 8 to 9). Piles are most frequently tested in axial compression (also in tension and laterally). Figure 9-1 shows the mechanism: (1) the pile is loaded incrementally from the head on a predetermined sequence or at a continuous, constant rate; (2) time, load and head movement are recorded, with strain measurements along the shaft for load transfer and unit shaft resistance; (3) a load-movement curve is plotted; (4) nominal resistance and the movement at it are determined by an interpretation method; (5) movement is usually measured at the head only, but telltales (solid rods in protective tubes, Figure 9-1) give movement anywhere along the pile; (6) telltales give strain between telltale points and strain gages at discrete points, both used to estimate load transfer.
key_points: Loading: incremental from the head, or continuous constant rate
Record time, load and head movement; plot the load-movement curve
Telltales and strain gages give movement and load transfer along the pile

sections.title: Compression Load Test Equipment
sections.summary: ASTM D1143 compression test equipment: jacking against an anchored beam or weighted platform; load cell primary, jack pressure secondary; spherical bearing plate; at least two gages (2 in. travel, 0.01 in. precision; 4 in. and 0.001 in. preferred); wire backup and survey level; 5 diameters and 8 ft clear distances.
sections.body: 9.2.2 Compression Load Test Equipment (pp. 9 to 14). ASTM D1143-07 (re-approved 2013) gives alternative systems for applying load and measuring movement. Loads are most often applied by jacking against a beam anchored by piles or ground anchors, or against a weighted platform. The primary load measurement should be a calibrated load cell, with jack pressure from a calibrated gage recorded as a secondary means; include a spherical bearing plate to minimize eccentricity. Head movement: LVDTs or dial gages between the pile head and an independently supported reference beam; ASTM requires at least 2 inches of travel and 0.01 inch precision, but at least 4 inches travel (especially for long piles with large elastic deformation) and 0.001 inch precision are highly recommended; at least two gages equidistant and diametrically opposite, four in opposite pairs often advantageous. Provide a redundant scale, mirror and wire system (0.01 inch precision) on two opposite faces, reference beams and wire independently supported at least 5 pile diameters and not less than 8 feet from the test and reaction piles, and a survey level as remote backup (also monitoring reaction piles). ASTM D1143: test-to-reaction pile clear distance at least 5 times the larger maximum diameter but not less than 8 feet; with a weighted platform, cribbing more than 5 feet from the test pile. Figure 9-2 is a typical setup schematic and Figures 9-3 and 9-4 show load application and movement monitoring; steel bearing plates should sit between the jack ram and load cell and between the load cell and spherical bearing plate (as in Figure 9-5; Section 9.6). Figure 9-5: MnDOT mobile load frame on reaction piles in a heated winter enclosure with wood reference beams to limit temperature effects. Figures 9-6 (reaction piles) and 9-7 (weighted platform) show typical arrangements. Record load and movement remotely so personnel are well away from the loading system.
key_points: Load cell is the primary load measurement; jack pressure gage is secondary; include a spherical bearing plate
Gages: ASTM minimum 2 in. travel, 0.01 in. precision; 4 in. travel and 0.001 in. precision recommended
Wire-mirror-scale backup and survey level; reference supports >= 5 diameters and >= 8 ft from piles
Test-to-reaction pile clear distance >= 5 diameters, not less than 8 ft; platform cribbing > 5 ft away
Bearing plates between jack ram, load cell and spherical plate; record readings remotely

sections.title: Recommended Axial Compression Test Loading Method
sections.summary: Quick load test (AASHTO 2014, ASTM D1143): 5% increments of anticipated nominal resistance (about 20 points), holds of 4 to 15 minutes, readings at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 (8, 15) minutes; unload in 5 to 10 decrements.
sections.body: 9.2.3 Recommended Axial Compression Test Loading Method (pp. 14 to 15). Standardized procedures must be followed; ASTM D1143 details several. AASHTO (2014) recommends the quick load test, which typically takes 2 to 4 hours, reducing delay and cost. Load increments are 5% of the anticipated nominal geotechnical resistance, giving on the order of 20 data points before nominal resistance. Each increment is held no more than 15 and no less than 4 minutes, the same interval for all; load and gross movement are read at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 minutes, with 8 and 15 minute readings for longer holds. Continue to nominal resistance or jack capacity within safe structural limits of pile and reaction. ASTM D1143 allows a longer hold at nominal resistance to assess creep, not feasible after plunging; if plunging occurs, lock off the pump and let the system reach equilibrium under the maximum resisted load. Then unload in 5 to 10 equal decrements, each held 4 to 15 minutes, read at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 (and 8 and 15) minutes, including zero load, which may be held longer for rebound. Figures 9-6 (4000-ton Caltrans mobile load frame) and 9-7 (weighted platform), referred to in 9.2.2, are printed in this section's pages.
key_points: Quick test (AASHTO 2014): typically 2 to 4 hours
Increments of 5% of anticipated nominal resistance, about 20 points to failure
Hold each increment 4 to 15 minutes; read at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 (8, 15) minutes
If plunging, lock off the pump; unload in 5 to 10 equal decrements

sections.title: Presentation and Interpretation of Axial Compression Test Results
sections.summary: Davisson offset limit interpretation (AASHTO 2014 Article 10.7.3.8.2): elastic line Delta = QL/AE (Eq. 9-1); failure at s_f = Delta + (0.15 + b/120) for b <= 24 in. (Eq. 9-2), Delta + b/30 for b > 36 in. (Eq. 9-3), interpolated between; for holds of 1 hour or less; factored resistance 0.75 to 0.80 of nominal.
sections.body: 9.2.4 Presentation and Interpretation of Axial Compression Test Results (pp. 16 to 19). Report per ASTM D1143 and plot a load-movement curve (Figure 9-8). Methods based on maximum allowable gross movement that ignore elastic deformation are not recommended (they overestimate short-pile and underestimate long-pile resistance); failure-criterion methods that include elastic deformation are better. AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.3.8.2 gives three criteria by pile size, all including elastic deformation; scales are chosen so the elastic line is inclined about 20 degrees from the load axis. Elastic deformation of a uniform pile: Delta = QL/AE (Eq. 9-1). The methods are Davisson (1972) offset limits: the intersection of the load-movement curve with an offset line parallel to the elastic line is the nominal resistance (failure load), a limiting deformation criterion; if not intersected, nominal resistance exceeds the maximum test load. For piles 24 inches or less: s_f = Delta + (0.15 + b/120) (Eq. 9-2); larger than 36 inches (more toe movement needed): s_f = Delta + b/30 (Eq. 9-3); between, interpolate linearly. b is the diameter or side width; for H-piles use the flange width. Davisson applies to increments held not more than 1 hour; long holds underestimate resistance. Compare primary (load cell) and back-up (jack pressure) loads throughout (the text cites 'Section 9.2.1', which is not printed; the systems are in 9.2.2); for large early discrepancies stop, find the cause (above-ground strain gages can show which is right), unload, correct and restart, since using the lower value risks overloading the jack, pile or reaction and the higher may end the test early or understate resistance. Factored compression resistance is 0.75 (static test only) to 0.80 (with dynamic testing and signal matching) of nominal. Head load-movement alone gives no load transfer; see Section 9.5.
key_points: Do not use gross-movement criteria that ignore elastic deformation
Elastic deformation Delta = QL/AE (Eq. 9-1); elastic line plotted about 20 degrees from the load axis
b <= 24 in.: s_f = Delta + (0.15 + b/120) (Eq. 9-2); b > 36 in.: s_f = Delta + b/30 (Eq. 9-3); interpolate between
H-piles: use flange width for b; Davisson valid for load holds not over 1 hour
Resolve load cell vs. jack pressure discrepancies before continuing
Factored compression resistance 0.75 to 0.80 of the failure load

sections.title: Limitations of Axial Compression Tests
sections.summary: Compression tests do not capture long-term settlement, downdrag or group action; other shortcomings are cost, time, little driving stress or damage information, misleading results in variable soils, and cost of load transfer gages.
sections.body: 9.2.5 Limitations of Axial Compression Tests (p. 19). Compression tests are the most accurate way to determine nominal resistance, but cannot account for long-term settlement, downdrag from consolidating soils, or pile group action. Other shortcomings: test cost, setup and test time, minimal information on driving stresses or damage, misleading results on highly variable sites, and significant added cost of strain gage instrumentation for load transfer.
key_points: Do not represent long-term settlement, downdrag or group action
Cost, time, little driving stress or damage information; misleading on highly variable sites
sections.applicability: Limitations of axial compression static pile load tests.

sections.title: Tension Load Test
sections.summary: Tension tests determine uplift resistance, often governing minimum penetration for groups with large uplift (cofferdam seal buoyancy, cantilever segmental construction, seismic, vessel impact, debris); often economical with crane mat reactions.
sections.body: 9.3 Tension Load Test (p. 20). Tension load tests determine axial tension (uplift) resistance, often significant for minimum penetration of groups with large uplift demand, including cofferdam seals with large buoyancy, cantilever segmental bridge construction, and seismic, vessel impact or debris loading. Mechanics are similar to compression tests with tension loading; tests are often economical, jacking against a reaction beam on crane mats rather than reaction piles.
key_points: Tension tests determine uplift resistance, often governing minimum penetration
Often economical: reaction beam on crane mats instead of reaction piles
sections.applicability: Static tension (uplift) load tests on driven piles.

sections.title: Tension Load Test Equipment
sections.summary: ASTM D3689 tension test equipment: jack on reaction beams over piles or mats; center hole jack with rod (concrete piles) or yoke (steel piles); load cell primary; spherical bearing plate; two gages (2 in. travel required, 4 in. recommended); wire backup and survey level; 5 diameters and 8 ft clearances.
sections.body: 9.3.1 Tension Load Test Equipment (pp. 20 to 21). ASTM D3689-07 (re-approved 2013) covers static axial tensile tests. Loads are most often applied by a hydraulic jack centered on reaction beams supported by reaction piles or by mats and cribbing on the ground. A center hole jack with a rod embedded in the pile passing between the beams and through the jack is common for concrete piles with low tension loads; a yoke with rods on either side of the beam(s) connected to the pile and a beam on the jack is common for steel piles. Load cell primary, calibrated jack pressure backup, spherical bearing plate. Movement by dial gages or LVDTs to an independent reference beam: ASTM requires at least 2 inches travel and 0.01 inch precision; 4 inches recommended; at least two gages equidistant and diametrically opposite; scale-mirror-wire backup (0.01 inch) on two opposite faces; supports at least 5 pile diameters and not less than 8 feet clear; survey level remote backup. Figure 9-9 shows a nearshore test with reaction beam and piles, Figure 9-10 a land test with beam on crane mats and timber cribbing.
key_points: Jack on reaction beams supported by piles or by mats and cribbing
Center hole jack with embedded rod (concrete piles) or yoke with rods (steel piles)
Gages: 2 in. travel and 0.01 in. precision required, 4 in. recommended; two opposite gages
Reference supports >= 5 diameters and >= 8 ft clear; wire backup and survey level
sections.applicability: Specifying equipment for a pile tension (uplift) load test.

sections.title: Tension Test Loading Methods
sections.summary: Quick test for tension (ASTM D3689): 5% increments (about 20 points), equal holds of 4 to 15 minutes, readings at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 (8, 15) minutes, unload in 5 to 10 decrements; test to pullout failure where possible; redrive tested production piles.
sections.body: 9.3.2 Tension Test Loading Methods (pp. 21 to 22). ASTM D3689 details several procedures; the Quick Test with increments of 5% of the anticipated nominal tension resistance (about 20 data points) is recommended, all increments held the same interval of 4 to 15 minutes. Read load and gross movement at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 minutes (8 and 15 for longer holds), continuing to nominal resistance or jack capacity within safe structural limits; after holding the maximum or reaching pullout failure, unload in 5 to 10 equal decrements held 4 to 15 minutes with the same readings, including zero load. Testing to geotechnical pullout failure is generally desirable, particularly in design stage programs; production piles tested in construction should be redriven to the original toe elevation and previous driving resistance. Figures 9-9 (pipe pile with reaction piles, Besix) and 9-10 (H-pile with mats and cribbing, WKG2) are printed in this section's pages.
key_points: Quick test: 5% increments of anticipated nominal tension resistance, equal holds of 4 to 15 minutes
Unload in 5 to 10 equal decrements, including a zero load reading
Test to pullout failure where possible; redrive tested production piles to original toe and resistance

sections.title: Presentation and Interpretation of Tension Test Results
sections.summary: Tension test interpretation: no widely accepted method; AASHTO (2014) uses a modified Davisson criterion, elastic lengthening plus a 0.15 inch offset; factored tension resistance 0.60 of the failure load.
sections.body: 9.3.3 Presentation and Interpretation of Tension Test Results (p. 23). Report per ASTM D3689 with a load-movement curve (Figure 9-11). No widely accepted method for nominal tension resistance has been published; Fuller (1983) reported criteria limiting gross or net upward movement, the curve's slope, or an offset limit with elastic lengthening plus an offset. AASHTO (2014) recommends a modified Davisson method: the load where the curve intersects elastic lengthening plus 0.15 inches is the nominal tension resistance (failure load); factored tension resistance is 0.60 of it.
key_points: No widely accepted tension failure criterion (Fuller 1983 lists several)
AASHTO (2014): elastic lengthening plus 0.15 in. offset defines the failure load
Factored tension resistance = 0.60 x failure load

sections.title: Lateral Load Test
sections.summary: Lateral tests are usually on single free-head piles while service piles are fixed-head groups, so their main purpose is to determine or verify p-y curves; often economical by jacking or pulling between two piles, possibly of different types.
sections.body: 9.4 Lateral Load Test (p. 24). Lateral load tests are performed where piles carry significant lateral loads; their importance has grown with extreme event limit states (seismic, vessel impact) and greater use of noise walls and large overhead signs. Most tests are on a single free-head pile while service piles are mostly fixed-head groups, so results may not apply directly; the primary purpose is to determine design p-y curves or verify those used. Tests are often economical by jacking or pulling between two piles, which in design stage tests may be different types or sections, assessing two in one test.
key_points: Single free-head test results may not apply directly to fixed-head groups
Primary purpose: determine or verify design p-y curves
Jacking or pulling between two piles is economical; they may be two pile types
sections.applicability: Lateral load tests on driven piles and their use to select or verify p-y curves.

sections.title: Lateral Load Test Equipment
sections.summary: ASTM D3966 lateral test equipment: jack against a reaction or between two piles (pulling preferred, piles at least 20 ft or 20 diameters apart); load cell primary; spherical bearing plate unless pulling; gages with 3 in. travel; deflection versus depth by inclinometer or Shape Accel Array strongly recommended; else head rotation.
sections.body: 9.4.1 Lateral Load Test Equipment (pp. 24 to 28). ASTM D3966-07 (re-approved 2013) covers lateral tests. Loads are most often applied by a jack against a reaction (piles, deadman, weighted platform) or between two piles; pulling the piles together is preferred (a two-force member keeps alignment), but ASTM then requires a clear distance of not less than 20 feet or 20 pile diameters. Load cell primary, jack pressure backup; a spherical bearing plate is required unless loading by pulling. Head movement by gages to a reference beam perpendicular to the movement: ASTM requires at least 3 inches travel and 0.01 inch precision; for a single pile one gage opposite the load point, with a scale-mirror-wire backup (0.01 inch) on the pile top or a bracket on the load line. Deflection versus depth is strongly recommended: inclinometer casing to below any lateral movement, read immediately after applying or removing an increment held 30 minutes or longer, or a Shape Accel Array (SSA); Kyfor et al. (1992) note head-only tests are seldom justifiable (see also ASTM D3966, FHWA-SA-91-042). Figure 9-12: 14 and 16 inch O.D. concrete filled pipe piles pushed apart, jack at the right pile and load cell with spherical bearing plate at the left (Figures 9-13, 9-14), each with in-place inclinometer strings (Figure 9-15). SSAs (Rollins et al. 2009): triaxial accelerometers in 1 inch PVC casing, recoverable, static and dynamic displacements, 12 inch segments giving more detail than inclinometers (Figure 9-16). If deflection versus depth is not feasible, measure head rotation (deflection at two elevations above the load point, or an inclinometer probe or tiltmeter) to assess p-y modelling.
key_points: Jack against a reaction or between two piles; pulling preferred, then >= 20 ft or 20 diameters apart
Load cell primary; spherical bearing plate unless loading by pulling
Head gages: ASTM minimum 3 in. travel, 0.01 in. precision
Measure deflection versus depth (inclinometer or Shape Accel Array); head-only tests seldom justifiable
If depth profile not feasible, measure pile head rotation

sections.title: Lateral Test Loading Methods
sections.summary: ASTM D3966 Standard Loading: total 200% of the lateral design load in decreasing increments, holds from 10 to 60 minutes, unload in four decrements with 10 minute holds (Table 9-2: 50% of design load each); readings before and after each change and every 5 minutes; 15 and 30 minutes after removal.
sections.body: 9.4.2 Lateral Test Loading Methods (pp. 28 to 29). ASTM D3966 details several procedures. The Standard Loading procedure takes the total test load to 200% of the proposed lateral design load, with increments decreasing as load increases and holds increasing from 10 minutes early to 60 minutes at maximum; unloading is in four decrements equal to 50% of the maximum (as printed) with 10 minute holds. Table 9-2 (after ASTM D3966), percent of design load and duration in minutes: 0 (-), 25 (10), 50 (10), 75 (15), 100 (20), 125 (20), 150 (20), 170 (20), 180 (20), 190 (20), 200 (60), 150 (10), 100 (10), 50 (10), 0 (30). Read load and gross movement immediately before and after each change and at 5 minute intervals; after removal at 15 and 30 minutes.
key_points: Standard Loading: total test load 200% of the proposed lateral design load
Holds 10 minutes early to 60 minutes at 200%; unloading with 10 minute holds
Read before and after each change, every 5 minutes, and 15 and 30 minutes after removal

sections.title: Presentation and Interpretation of Lateral Test Results
sections.summary: Lateral test interpretation is more complex: report head load-deflection (Figure 9-17) and deflection versus depth (Figure 9-18), compare with p-y software predictions (Figure 9-19) to set or verify design p-y curves.
sections.body: 9.4.3 Presentation and Interpretation of Lateral Test Results (pp. 29 to 31). Report per ASTM D3966; interpretation is much more complicated than for axial tests. Figure 9-17 shows a typical head load-deflection curve; with depth measurements, report deflection versus depth (Figure 9-18) and compare with p-y software predictions (Figure 9-19, measured vs. COM624P, after Kyfor et al. 1992). The comparison sets the p-y curves for design (design stage) or checks those used (construction stage). See FHWA IP 84 11 (Reese 1984) and FHWA-SA-91-042 (Kyfor et al. 1992).

sections.title: Load Transfer Evaluations
sections.summary: Shaft and toe resistances and unit shaft resistances come from instrumented static load tests using telltale rods (extensometers) or surface mounted or embedded strain gages.
sections.body: 9.5 Load Transfer Evaluations (p. 32). The magnitude of shaft and toe resistances or unit shaft resistances can be determined from instrumented static load tests, using telltale rods (extensometers) or surface mounted or embedded strain gages, discussed in the following sections.
key_points: Load transfer from telltales (extensometers) or strain gages in instrumented static tests
sections.applicability: Load transfer from instrumented static load tests: telltales, strain gages, residual load.

sections.title: Use of Telltales
sections.summary: Telltales: Q_avg = AE (R1 - R2)/L (Eq. 9-4); with head and toe readings, toe resistance R_p = 2Q_avg - Q for uniform shaft resistance (Eq. 9-5) or 3Q_avg - 2Q for triangular (Eq. 9-6); shaft resistance = Q - R_p.
sections.body: 9.5.1 Use of Telltales (pp. 32 to 34). Telltales are thin steel rods from the pile head to a selected point, encased in a slightly larger tube (Figure 9-20); NYSDOT GCP-18 (2007) gives details for pipe, H and timber piles. Gages on the rod tops measure movement relative to the reference beam or pile head; differences between rod attachment points give load transfer. Kyfor et al. (1992): average load between two points Q_avg = AE (R1 - R2)/L (Eq. 9-4), with R1 and R2 the upper and lower readings and L the length between points under no load. With R1 at the head and R2 at the toe, Fellenius (1990): for uniform shaft resistance, toe resistance R_p = 2Q_avg - Q (Eq. 9-5); for linearly increasing (triangular) resistance, R_p = 3Q_avg - 2Q (Eq. 9-6); Q is the head test load chosen as close to the failure load as possible. Shaft resistance = head load minus toe resistance.
key_points: Telltale rods in tubes measure movement at selected points (NYSDOT GCP-18 details)
Q_avg = AE (R1 - R2)/L between two measuring points (Eq. 9-4)
Toe resistance: R_p = 2Q_avg - Q uniform (Eq. 9-5); R_p = 3Q_avg - 2Q triangular (Eq. 9-6)
Use the head load closest to the failure load; shaft resistance = Q - R_p

sections.title: Use of Strain Gages
sections.summary: Strain gages for detailed load transfer: vibrating wire gages (welded on steel, sister bars in concrete) or resistance gages; top gages at least two diameters below the head in a resistance-free zone; F = eps E A (Eq. 9-7); composite E (Eq. 9-8); tangent modulus method for concrete (Eqs. 9-9 to 9-12).
sections.body: 9.5.2 Use of Strain Gages (pp. 34 to 41). Telltales alone miss residual load, so detailed load transfer needs strain gages. Dunnicliff (1988): weldable vibrating wire gages on steel piles and sister bars with vibrating wire gages in concrete piles; other types if static and dynamic measurements are wanted; an instrumentation specialist should select gages that survive handling and driving, redundancy and data acquisition. Figures 9-21 (sister bars, tied to rebar or to a centralized bar in pipe piles), 9-22 (arc-weldable gage between welded blocks on an H-pile), 9-23 (bolt-on waterproof foil gage under a steel channel on a pipe pile), 9-24 (resistance gages on sister bars with an accelerometer, in a casting bed). Moisture is a leading cause of resistance gage failure: check and seal lead wires; a multichannel data acquisition system is needed. Locate gages by the nearest boring to get unit shaft resistance in chosen strata, plus extra for redundancy. The top gage should be in a zone without shaft resistance: Dunnicliff recommends three undamaged diameters above ground; at minimum two diameters below the head for full load development, where modulus can be found and internal versus external readings show composite action of concrete filled pipe (Sellers 1995; Komurka 2015); use gage pairs or centralizers against bending (Figure 9-25). Komurka (2015) also recommends gages two diameters above the toe to extrapolate toe resistance; sister bars near the toe of pipe piles should hang from the head during curing, not rest on the toe. Force F = eps E A (Eq. 9-7); for concrete filled steel, E = (E_st A_st + E_c A_c)/(A_st + A_c) (Eq. 9-8). Concrete modulus falls with strain, so Fellenius (2001) recommends the Tangent Modulus Method: plot tangent modulus versus microstrain for all gages and increments, fit M_t = Delta_sigma/Delta_eps = A eps + B (Eq. 9-9, Figure 9-26), integrate to sigma = (A/2) eps^2 + B eps (Eq. 9-10); with sigma = E_sm eps (Eq. 9-11), E_sm = 0.5 A eps + B (Eq. 9-12). Example (Figure 9-27, seven gages, 14 inch concrete filled pipe): 53.9 - 37.6 = 16.3 tons between EL 549.7 and EL 537.4, 12.3 ft apart, 3.67 ft circumference: 16.3/45.1 ft2 = 0.36 tsf, ignoring residual load (Section 9.5.3). Unit shaft resistances can assess similar piles (e.g., 12 or 16 inch) or refine penetration depth.
key_points: Strain gages needed for detailed load transfer (telltales miss residual load)
Vibrating wire: welded on steel piles, sister bars in concrete; resistance gages also for dynamic data
Top gages at least 2 diameters below the head in a resistance-free zone; paired against bending
Gages 2 diameters above the toe to extrapolate toe resistance (Komurka 2015)
F = eps E A (Eq. 9-7); composite modulus (Eq. 9-8); tangent modulus method (Eqs. 9-9 to 9-12)

sections.title: Determination of Residual Load
sections.summary: Residual load locked in during driving makes shaft resistance appear too large (up to twice) and toe resistance too small; total nominal resistance is unaffected. Zero gages before installation; Fellenius (2002b) method to estimate the true resistance distribution.
sections.body: 9.5.3 Determination of Residual Load (pp. 41 to 46). Residual loads remain in piles that do not fully rebound after a blow, especially flexible piles and piles with large shaft resistance or toe quake. Telltale evaluations assume none, so the load distribution 'calculated from Eq. 9-5 to 9-7' (as printed) excludes it, and with R1 and R2 at head and toe the average load includes it, giving a lower toe resistance than actual (Figure 9-28). With residual load, negative shaft resistance acts on the upper pile and must be overcome first. Fellenius (2014), Figure 9-29: without residual load shaft resistance follows O-B-C; with it the pile is first loaded along D-A and the test follows A-O-B-C, so ignoring it (A-B-C) measures shaft resistance twice the true value. Toe (Figure 9-30): O-B-C without, A-D-B-C with residual load, so toe resistance develops before the test; unloading follows B-D'-A; residual load leads to underestimating toe resistance. Geotechnical nominal resistance is unaffected but shaft and toe values change, which matters for uplift taken from compression test shaft resistance or unit values used in design. Zero readings must be taken before installation (factory readings for sister bars). Fellenius et al. (2003): the strain difference just before the test and at true no load is a lower bound, possibly an underestimate with thermal strains in hydrating concrete. Fellenius (2002b) case (Figure 9-31, prestressed pile driven 48 ft in loose to medium dense uniform sand; Altaee et al. 1992): the measured load curve inflects near 23 ft, implying smaller unit shaft resistance in the bottom third, so residual load is likely. Plot measured shaft resistance divided by 2 versus depth; the True Resistance follows it to the inflection and is extrapolated below assuming the same unit resistance; residual load = True Resistance minus Measured Load. Judgment and careful interpretation are needed.
key_points: Residual load from driving: common in flexible piles and those with large shaft resistance or toe quake
Ignoring it can double the apparent shaft resistance and understate toe resistance
Nominal (total) resistance unaffected; shaft/toe split and unit values are
Zero gage readings before installation (factory readings for sister bars)
Fellenius (2002b): measured shaft resistance / 2 to the inflection, extrapolate below

sections.title: Practical Issues and Considerations
sections.summary: Static load tests are the most reliable and most expensive method; avoid delays by deciding early and specifying tests before ordering lengths; resolve load cell versus jack pressure discrepancies (10% to 20% in Fellenius 1984); match jack and load cell sizes and use thick bearing plates (Geokon 2013).
sections.body: 9.6 Practical Issues and Considerations (pp. 46 to 48). Static load tests are the most reliable and most expensive method for nominal resistance or lateral deformation; cost alone should not decide, and instrumentation specialists should be involved. Delays usually come from adding tests late: decide early in design; in construction specify the number and locations of tests and the engineer's review time, and require tests before ordering pile lengths or production driving. Fellenius (1984): in a retest after replacing the load cell and recalibrating, jack pressure exceeded the load cell by 10% to 20% in loading and underestimated by 5% in unloading (Figure 9-32); find the cause of disagreement and rerun if needed. Size load cells and jacks to reduce error: Geokon (2013) found error when load cell and jack piston diameters differ, compounded by thin bearing plates; a 4 inch I.D., 5-3/4 inch O.D., 300 kip load cell was used with jacks of 2 x 4, 4 x 5-3/4 and 6 x 8 inch I.D. x O.D. (Figure 9-33).
key_points: Most reliable and most expensive method; cost alone should not decide
Specify number, location and review time; test before ordering lengths or production driving
Jack pressure differed from load cell by 10% to 20% loading, 5% unloading (Fellenius 1984)

sections.title: Advantages, Disadvantages, and Limitations
sections.summary: Advantages: more rational design, possible shorter piles or higher loads, resistance factors 0.75 to 0.80 versus 0.40 for Modified Gates, confirmation at planned penetration. Disadvantages: cost, time, little stress or damage data, misleading in variable soils. Limitations: no long-term settlement, downdrag or group action.
sections.body: 9.7 Advantages, Disadvantages, and Limitations (pp. 48 to 49). Advantages: (1) more rational design; static tests are considerably more reliable than static analyses and dynamic formulas; (2) better knowledge of pile-soil behavior may allow shorter piles or higher factored loads; (3) a higher resistance factor, 0.75 to 0.80 with static load tests versus 0.40 for the Modified Gates dynamic formula; (4) confirmation that the factored load is supported at the planned penetration. Disadvantages: test cost, setup and test time, interpretation time (especially with load transfer data), minimal information on driving stresses or damage, and misleading results on highly variable sites, so consider site size and variability before relying on one test pile. Limitations: results cannot account for long-term settlement, downdrag from consolidating soils, or group action.
